item.title: Fiji braces for extended strong winds
item.description: A PROLONGED spell of gusty weather will continue to sweep across Fiji, with rough maritime conditions persisting well into next week, says Fiji Meteorological Services forecaster Shivneel Prasad. Mr Prasad said residents should prepare for ongoing squalls following the latest weather bulletin.
item.content:encoded:
A PROLONGED spell of gusty weather will continue to sweep across Fiji, with rough maritime conditions persisting well into next week, says Fiji Meteorological Services forecaster Shivneel Prasad.

Mr Prasad said residents should prepare for ongoing squalls following the latest weather bulletin.

“In terms of weather, I do not expect much change, just a bit of windy conditions to continue.”

Mr Prasad said that southeast winds will bring noticeably cooler nights to the group.

The primary concern remains focused on maritime safety, as strong wind warnings cover all Fijian waters.

Mr Prasad strongly caution mariners against taking unnecessary risks in open ocean areas.

“Definitely with the strong wind warnings, small boats are not recommended to be out at sea.”

Mr Prasad said rough seas present severe hazards for smaller boats , adding that its easy for them to be lifted further away, especially if they have any engine troubles.

While the current warning may briefly lift early next week, another surge of strong winds is expected just half a day later.

Mr Prasad said only isolated showers might affect parts of the country on Friday and Saturday, leaving many areas completely dry.

item.title: Ravunawa: Women increasingly being affected
item.description: THE rise in HIV infections among women is becoming a growing concern for Fiji, says the Assistant Health Minister Penioni Ravunawa. Mr Ravunawa said women were increasingly being affected by the country’s HIV epidemic.
item.content:encoded:
THE rise in HIV infections among women is becoming a growing concern for Fiji, says the Assistant Health Minister Penioni Ravunawa.

Mr Ravunawa said women were increasingly being affected by the country’s HIV epidemic.

“Approximately 94 per cent of new diagnoses are among our iTaukei population, while infections among women are also increasing,” he said.

He said the figures should not be viewed simply as statistics because every diagnosis affected a person and their family.

“Behind every diagnosis is a person. Behind every person is a family.”

He said Fiji needed to ensure women had access to information, testing, prevention and treatment services without fear or stigma.

He urged young people to make HIV testing a normal part of healthcare.

“There should be no shame in getting tested and no stigma attached to knowing your status.”

He said women who tested positive should seek treatment early, while those who tested negative should take steps to remain negative.

“Stigma and discrimination could prevent people from seeking testing and treatment.

“Fight HIV. Fight misinformation. Fight stigma, but never fight the person living with HIV.”

He said protecting women from HIV was essential to protecting families and communities.

item.title: Mothers must be at heart of HIV prevention, says advocate
item.description: ELIMINATING vertical transmission of HIV requires healthcare systems to focus as much on the mother’s holistic wellbeing as they do on the baby’s safety, says prominent advocate Rebecca Kubunavanua. Speaking at the 2026 Pacific HIV Symposium at the Sheraton Fiji Golf Resort and Spa yesterday, Ms Kubunavanua emphasised that clinical tools alone cannot achieve long-term success without addressing th
item.content:encoded:
ELIMINATING vertical transmission of HIV requires healthcare systems to focus as much on the mother’s holistic wellbeing as they do on the baby’s safety, says prominent advocate Rebecca Kubunavanua.

Speaking at the 2026 Pacific HIV Symposium at the Sheraton Fiji Golf Resort and Spa yesterday, Ms Kubunavanua emphasised that clinical tools alone cannot achieve long-term success without addressing the human element of healthcare.

“Success is not simply an HIV-negative baby, but success is a healthy baby, a healthy and supportive mother, and a woman who feels respected throughout the journey,” she said.

A woman living with HIV herself, Ms Kubunavanua highlighted how the complex pregnancy cascade often fails mothers after delivery.

While early antenatal care, early diagnosis, and antiretroviral therapy (ART) drastically reduce transmission risks, systemic barriers such as fear of disclosure, financial pressures, transport challenges, and social stigma frequently cause women to drop out of continuous care.

Ms Kubunavanua said health services must actively integrate peer support into formal clinical pathways to bridge the gap between diagnosis and everyday life.

Community-led support provides the essential trust, emotional backup, and guidance that clinical settings often lack.

“Instead of asking why didn’t she comply, perhaps we should ask what happened that made it difficult for her to stay connected to care and how can we help.”

To strengthen national healthcare frameworks, Ms Kubunavanua outlined five priority actions: making antenatal contacts safe spaces, embedding peer support into clinical pathways, measuring the full care cascade, protecting confidentiality, and maintaining robust postnatal support.

She stressed that policies must directly involve women living with HIV

item.title: 646 young adults diagnosed with HIV
item.description: YOUNG adults and children represent a alarming proportion of Fiji’s growing HIV epidemic, threatening the nation’s socio-economic future and social stability Addressing delegates at the 2026 Pacific HIV Symposium in Nadi yesterday, President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu revealed that individuals aged between 20 and 24 accounted for 646 new diagnoses in 2025 representing nearly one in every three cases
item.content:encoded:
YOUNG adults and children represent a alarming proportion of Fiji’s growing HIV epidemic, threatening the nation’s socio-economic future and social stability

Addressing delegates at the 2026 Pacific HIV Symposium in Nadi yesterday, President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu revealed that individuals aged between 20 and 24 accounted for 646 new diagnoses in 2025 representing nearly one in every three cases recorded nationwide.

“And for the 646, most of them are young figures, entering adulthood, starting careers, forming relationships and families and carrying our country’s future,” he said.

“When an epidemic becomes so concentrated amongst young people, the consequences are not limited to the health sector.”

Ratu Naiqama said surveillance figures also highlighted a severe impact on pediatric health. In 2025, 67 children under the age of 15 were diagnosed with HIV, including 56 cases attributed directly to mother-to-child transmission.

He added that 17 HIV-related deaths were reported among children aged 0 to 14.

“Every preventable infection in a child must challenge us to examine the full chain of antenatal testing.”

item.title: Doctor calls for a unified regional response
item.description: PACIFIC Island nations must unite and share vital public health strategies to effectively combat the region’s rapidly growing HIV epidemic, health leaders heard in Nadi yesterday. Speaking at the 2026 Pacific HIV Symposium at the Sheraton Fiji Golf Resort and Spa, Interim Lead for the SRH and HIV unit Dr Jason Michell called for a unified regional response to the public health crisis.
item.content:encoded:
PACIFIC Island nations must unite and share vital public health strategies to effectively combat the region’s rapidly growing HIV epidemic, health leaders heard in Nadi yesterday.

Speaking at the 2026 Pacific HIV Symposium at the Sheraton Fiji Golf Resort and Spa, Interim Lead for the SRH and HIV unit Dr Jason Michell called for a unified regional response to the public health crisis.

Dr Michell said no single government or organisation could address the challenge in isolation, emphasizing that enduring responses are built through collaboration.

“When Fiji declared a national HIV outbreak last year, we did not have all the answers, and the truth is, we still don’t.

“But we have learned something true about every country here. No government, no ministry or community can solve HIV alone.”

While Fiji faces a rapidly growing epidemic and Papua New Guinea continues to face enormous challenges, Dr Mitchell said epidemiology was changing across the entire region.

The two-day symposium was established out of necessity and hope, aiming to create a platform where islands can benefit from shared knowledge on prevention, treatment, and stigma reduction.

“If one island discovers a better way of preventing HIV, keep people on treatment or reduce stigma, every island should benefit from that knowledge.

“That is the purpose of these two days, not simply to exchange presentations and share data, but to build a stronger Pacific response together.”

Dr Michell urged participants to approach the summit with openness, focusing on practical frontline solutions for clinicians, peer workers, and policymakers.

“I ask all of us to make this a place of honesty, for learning, not blaming, for reflection, not criticism, and for preparedness, not panic.

“Share your successes, but also share the failures openly.”

item.title: Ravunawa sets record straight | Proposed needle program
item.description: THE proposed needle and syringe program is not to encourage drug use but to reduce the spread of HIV and other blood-borne infections. This was raised by the Assistant Health Minister Penioni Ravunawa as there had been claims made that Government would encourage drug use with the roll out of the program.
item.content:encoded:
THE proposed needle and syringe program is not to encourage drug use but to reduce the spread of HIV and other blood-borne infections.

This was raised by the Assistant Health Minister Penioni Ravunawa as there had been claims made that Government would encourage drug use with the roll out of the program.

“Let me be very clear, the needle and syringe program does not promote drug use,” he said.

Mr Ravunawa said the program was being progressed as part of the Government’s response to Fiji’s rapidly escalating HIV epidemic.

“It is designed to reduce harm, prevent the sharing of contaminated injecting equipment, and reduce the transmission of HIV and other blood-borne infections.

He said most of the HIV cases were spread through the sharing of needles and syringes.

“We cannot ignore risky behaviour simply because it is uncomfortable to discuss.”

He said the program would need to form part of a wider response involving counselling, HIV testing, treatment, safe disposal, rehabilitation pathways, peer support and community education.

“Appropriate engagement with law-enforcement agencies would also be required.

“Our responsibility as Government is to protect life, prevent disease and reduce harm.”

He said the program was not a stand-alone solution and must be supported by other HIV prevention measures.

Fiji recorded 2016 new HIV cases in 2025, compared with 245 in 2022.

item.title: Malimali fires back | Former FICAC chief accuses leaders of ‘jumping the gun
item.description: FORMER FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali has launched a blistering attack on senior political leaders, accusing them of jumping to conclusions, making statements without evidence and wasting millions of dollars of taxpayers’ money in the legal battle surrounding her appointment. Her comments came as she was asked about Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s decision to appeal against certain aspects o
item.content:encoded:
FORMER FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali has launched a blistering attack on senior political leaders, accusing them of jumping to conclusions, making statements without evidence and wasting millions of dollars of taxpayers’ money in the legal battle surrounding her appointment.

Her comments came as she was asked about Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s decision to appeal against certain aspects of a recent High Court ruling that declared the findings of a Commission of Inquiry into her appointment null and void.

Ms Malimali said Mr Rabuka had every right to appeal.

“That’s well within his rights, and I wish him well,” she said.

But she questioned whether the public cost of the proceedings was justified.

“I think some of that money could be better utilised to assist our people,” she said, pointing to people travelling to Kadavu and Fiji’s outer islands.

“I think our taxpayers and our citizens deserve services that are better than what we’re currently having.”

“That kind of money should actually be spent where it’s needed — on schools and hospitals.”

“Some of our children need more. Not Barbara Malimali.”

She said she would be able to support herself regardless of the outcome.

“Barbara Malimali loses her job today, goes and works for herself tomorrow.”

Ms Malimali also took direct aim at political statements made about her, particularly claims that she had treated senior politicians differently while serving in public office.

“I mean, how much more wrong could they have been.

“This is the kind of mess that our leaders get ourselves into. They jump the gun. They make statements without thinking. They make statements not based on evidence.”

Her criticism was not limited to the current appeal.

She said she believed the wider controversy began because a group of people did not want her to become FICAC Commissioner.

“They realised I shouldn’t — I was not the person they wanted in FICAC.”

She also defended her record as Electoral Commission chair, maintaining that the decisions she made were based on the Constitution.

“Would I change anything? No. I didn’t do anything wrong.”
